impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that claims directed to humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating a jury verdict that Eli Lilly willfully infringed Teva's headache patents covering anti-CGRP antibody treatments. The case has major implications for the scope of written-description and enablement requirements for biologic and antibody patents, particularly where the specification discloses one species and known methods of making others within a claimed genus.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens the ability of pharmaceutical and biotech companies to obtain and enforce genus claims for antibody patents where the specification discloses representative species and known methods, providing broader patent protection for biologics.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies developing competing biologic therapies face increased risk of infringement liability where patent holders can enforce broad genus claims covering classes of antibodies based on limited specific disclosures.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions using emulation and function call models are directed to an abstract idea under Alice step one, and whether damages based on foreign sales of cybersecurity software were properly awarded.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict finding willful infringement of Columbia's cybersecurity patents by Norton, holding the claims abstract at Alice step one and remanding for step two analysis. The court also ruled that damages based on Norton's foreign sales were improperly awarded, reinforcing extraterritoriality limits on patent damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies facing patent infringement claims benefit from the court's rigorous application of Alice step one to cybersecurity and software patents, and the reinforcement of limits on damages for foreign sales narrows potential exposure.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the software and cybersecurity space face heightened risk that their claims will be found abstract under § 101, potentially reducing the value and enforceability of software-related patent portfolios.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive commercialization rights but retains the right to sue for infringement and other exclusionary rights has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue third parties for infringement possessed sufficient exclusionary rights to satisfy Article III standing. The decision clarifies standing requirements for patentees who partially license their patent rights.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners who structure licensing agreements to retain litigation rights can confidently enforce their patents against infringers, providing flexibility in licensing while preserving enforcement capability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential standing defense in cases where patent owners retain meaningful exclusionary rights despite granting broad exclusive licenses.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet brought suit, given evidence that Insulet knew or should have known of the alleged misappropriation more than three years before filing.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict and damages judgment in favor of Insulet on its DTSA trade secret misappropriation claim against EOFlow, holding that the three-year statute of limitations had expired before suit was filed. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation well before the limitations period.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's three-year limitations period, providing greater certainty and limiting stale claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must be vigilant in monitoring potential misappropriation and filing suit promptly; delay in bringing claims, even while investigating, risks losing the right to recover under the DTSA.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether legally sufficient evidence supported the jury's finding that the asserted information constituted protectable trade secrets under California law, and whether the same ideas could support an inventorship claim.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation and breach of contract claims, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the information was generally known. The court also reversed the patent invalidity finding based on inventorship, holding that contributions of generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from the court's rigorous analysis of whether asserted information truly qualifies as a protectable trade secret, particularly where the information is generally known in the field.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face increased burden to demonstrate that their claimed secrets are not generally known, and companies relying on trade secret protection for competitive advantage may find their claims vulnerable to challenge.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and properly struck damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure in damages contentions.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the grant of summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent against Intel, finding genuine issues of material fact on extraterritoriality and doctrine of equivalents. The court also reversed the striking of VLSI's damages expert theories, finding the district court applied an overly rigid disclosure standard.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the court's rejection of overly broad extraterritoriality defenses and more flexible treatment of damages expert disclosures, preserving their ability to reach trial on infringement and damages theories.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global operations face continued exposure to U.S. patent infringement claims even where key accused conduct occurs partly outside the United States.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a flawed jury verdict form that posed a single infringement question covering all asserted patents required vacatur, and whether the district court erred in its § 101 analysis of wireless building automation patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated an $11.5 million infringement and damages judgment in a building automation patent case, holding that a verdict form with a single infringement question covering all asserted patents was reversible error requiring a new trial. The court also vacated and remanded for further Alice step two analysis on the '495 patent while affirming eligibility of the '887 and '371 patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that verdict forms must separately identify infringement of each asserted patent, providing greater clarity and preventing bundled verdicts that obscure the basis for liability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders pursuing multi-patent infringement actions face increased procedural requirements for verdict forms and risk vacatur of favorable verdicts if infringement findings are not patent-specific.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices attached to farming equipment are patent-ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in finding the case not exceptional under § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patents were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, but vacated the determination that the case was not exceptional and remanded for reconsideration of attorney fees under § 285. The decision reinforces the vulnerability of agricultural technology and data-collection patents to § 101 challenges.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies accused of infringing data-collection and ag-tech patents can more readily challenge such claims as abstract under § 101, and prevailing defendants may obtain attorney fees in exceptional cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Ag-tech and IoT companies holding patents on data collection and processing systems face significant eligibility risk, potentially undermining patent portfolios in these growing sectors.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the jury's infringement and damages findings were supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain communication system patent claims while affirming eligibility for others, affirming infringement findings against LG, and affirming the damages award. The split eligibility determination provides important guidance on when specific technical implementations in communication standards satisfy § 101.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies holding patents on specific technical implementations incorporated into communication standards may find their claims eligible under § 101, supporting enforcement of standard-essential and related patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Electronics manufacturers implementing communication standards face continued patent infringement exposure, particularly where patents claim specific non-obvious technical implementations rather than abstract concepts.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate designee may testify at summary judgment about matters outside personal knowledge to establish the on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether computer source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of patent invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) deposition testimony may be considered at summary judgment even when the designee lacks personal knowledge, and that computer source code constituting machine commands is not hearsay. The decision has broad implications for how prior art evidence is presented in patent litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from relaxed evidentiary standards for proving prior art sales through corporate designee testimony and source code, making it easier to establish on-sale bar defenses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater vulnerability to invalidity challenges based on 30(b)(6) testimony from witnesses who lack personal knowledge of historical sales, and may find it harder to exclude source code evidence as hearsay.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple Watch blood oxygen measurement features infringed Masimo's wearable pulse oximetry patents and properly established a domestic industry.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's limited exclusion order barring importation of Apple Watches with blood oxygen features that infringe Masimo's wearable pulse oximetry patents. The court upheld the Commission's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, and infringement findings, sustaining a significant import ban on one of Apple's flagship products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the medical device and wearable technology space are affirmed in their ability to use ITC proceedings to obtain powerful exclusion orders against major competitors, even for features embedded in complex consumer electronics.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies integrating health-monitoring features into consumer devices face significant supply chain and product design disruption from ITC exclusion orders, and must carefully navigate existing patent landscapes when adding new functionalities.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay of a refiled declaratory judgment action under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) after having missed the deadline in an earlier-filed action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that a respondent in an ITC proceeding may not circumvent the mandatory stay deadline under § 1659(a) by dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action. The decision prevents gamesmanship in the parallel litigation between ITC proceedings and district court patent actions, particularly in pharmaceutical patent disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the closing of a potential loophole that ITC respondents could have exploited to delay or manipulate the timing of parallel district court proceedings.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the § 1659(a) stay deadline cannot cure the defect by refiling, requiring more careful attention to litigation timing and strategy when facing parallel ITC and district court proceedings.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a patent damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report and vacated summary judgment in favor of Microsoft, holding that the district court applied an improperly rigid standard in evaluating the expert's methodology. The decision reinforces that damages experts should not be excluded merely because their methodology requires refinement, and that summary judgment based solely on the absence of a quantified remedy is inappropriate.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from a more permissive standard for damages expert testimony, reducing the risk that technically complex damages theories will be excluded at the Daubert stage before reaching a jury.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a powerful tool for obtaining early case dispositions through Daubert challenges to damages experts, potentially increasing litigation costs and exposure.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, including approval of attorneys' fees and incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement in which the federal judiciary agreed to reimburse hundreds of thousands of PACER users for allegedly excessive fees. The court upheld the settlement terms, attorneys' fee awards, and incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives, rejecting objections to the district court's jurisdiction and the settlement's fairness.
impacts.positiveImplications: The settlement provides direct financial reimbursement to businesses and law firms that use PACER, and the ruling validates the use of class action settlements to address systemic government overcharges.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether surviving patent claims not directly addressed in an IPR can be dismissed as invalid on the same obviousness grounds applied to other claims of the same patent, and whether the resulting case qualified as exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of a patent infringement suit on obviousness grounds but reversed the exceptional case finding and attorney fee and sanction awards, holding that the district court's grounds were insufficient to support a conclusion of exceptionality or attorney bad faith. The decision clarifies the limits of § 285 fee-shifting and § 1927 sanctions in patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders and their counsel benefit from the court's higher threshold for exceptional case findings and sanctions, reducing the chilling effect of fee-shifting on patent enforcement efforts.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers who prevail on invalidity defenses face a higher bar to recover attorney fees even when the asserted claims appear weak in light of prior IPR proceedings.
